clue.text: Fighting en masse? You need protection

parts.note: en masse means in bulk, so the fighting goes inside the bulk
war is fighting on a large scale

explanation.surface: Someone warns that if a mass brawl breaks out you will want something to shelter behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'En masse' does two jobs: it means 'in bulk', which supplies both the outer word and the instruction to put the fighting inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulwark is a defensive wall or rampart, and figuratively any safeguard against harm.

clue.text: The good journalist worked hard when up

definitions.note: the answer means worked hard when followed by up, as in studied

parts.note: French for good, as in le bon
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A conscientious reporter put in long hours once he had climbed the ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: To bone up is to study intensively, so the answer means 'worked hard' only with 'up' after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bone up is an informal phrasal verb for cramming knowledge on a subject before an exam or task.

clue.text: Story about a sheep in a Western town

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the story wraps round the sheep

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A tale about a sheep set in a frontier settlement of the American West.
explanation.definitionFit: Laramie is a city in Wyoming, famous from cowboy films and the Western television series named after it.

clue.text: Setter's car won't start — it needs a service

indicators.note: a thing that won't start has lost its beginning, so the first letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
the setter refers to himself, so his is my

explanation.surface: The puzzle compiler's motor won't fire up and needs to go to the garage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests a car garage service; it means one of the armed services.
explanation.definitionFit: The army is one of the three armed services, alongside the navy and air force.

clue.text: Notice to visitors: avoid cannabis…

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the sign telling people not to walk on the lawn
second meaning: grass is slang for marijuana, so this is advice to stay away from it

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the next clue, also about drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the familiar park sign, and grass is a slang word for marijuana, so it also urges abstinence.

clue.text: Ancient poet's coming back almost wealthy

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the following word is dropped

parts.note: someone coming back is heading home
plain synonym

explanation.surface: An old bard is returning from his travels nearly rich.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 'poet's' is the definition read as an adjective: belonging to Homer.
explanation.definitionFit: Homeric describes anything relating to Homer, the Greek epic bard credited with the Iliad and Odyssey.

clue.text: …It's far from safe taking a 21 on the drug, as only E works

parts.note: 21 is a trip; someone on a drug trip is high

indicators.note: something that works is made or wrought, so these letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that dropping acid is risky, since only ecstasy actually works.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is TRIP, and being on a trip means being high. In a down clue 'on' puts that piece above the rest. E is ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Highly dangerous means extremely risky, the opposite end of the scale from safe.

clue.text: See 17
I abandon Netanyahu in the stampede? Nonsense!

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the shortened nickname goes within the stampede

parts.note: a stampede is a sudden rush

indicators.note: the letter I abandons the nickname, so one of its I's is removed

parts.note: Bibi is the nickname of the Israeli leader Binyamin Netanyahu

explanation.surface: Someone declares they are deserting the Israeli prime minister in a panicked rush, and is told that is absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish is the everyday British word for nonsense or worthless talk, as well as household waste.

clue.text: Clinton's flower show

definitions.note: the answer is Clinton's daughter, not a possessive
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the name of Bill Clinton's daughter
second meaning: the famous annual horticultural event held in a district of London

explanation.surface: It reads as a horticultural exhibition put on by the President.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chelsea Flower Show is a famous annual garden show in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill and Hillary Clinton's only child bears this name, as does the London district of the Royal Horticultural Society's yearly display.

clue.text: Engineers en masse? Good start for trial scene

parts.note: en masse means in number, so the engineers sit inside the number
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: opening letter of good

explanation.surface: A crowd of engineers turns up, which is a promising beginning for a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: As with 'en masse' elsewhere in this puzzle, the phrase is read as 'in number', putting the engineers inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The German city hosted the post-war tribunals of leading Nazis in 1945-46, the most famous trials of the century.

clue.text: Am I starting to be on good terms with the message?

indicators.note: the clue words Am I are the start of a longer word, and what remains after that start is the answer

parts.note: friendly, on good terms
taken as written, the letters that open the longer word

explanation.surface: Someone anxiously wonders whether they are beginning to get along with whoever sent the note.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says that AM I plus the answer makes AMICABLE, so the answer is AMICABLE with AMI taken off the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable is a telegram, a message sent by telegraph wire, especially overseas.

clue.text: Pantomime character in Britain and America

indicators.note: in says the answer lies inside the words that follow, spanning their letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of and and the start of America

explanation.surface: A stock pantomime figure appears on both sides of the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Britain and America' looks like geography; 'in' is the signal and the answer straddles two words. Pantomime is a British Christmas stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: In British pantomime the comic older woman, played by a man in drag, is the stock role with this title.

clue.text: English essays on Labour are like soaps

definitions.note: 'like soaps' means things such as soaps, a plural noun

parts.note: labour as hard work
standard abbreviation
an essay is an attempt

explanation.surface: A political comment: English compositions about the Labour Party are as melodramatic as TV soaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essays' and 'Labour' suggest school work and politics; they mean attempts and hard work. 'On' places the later pieces after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Toiletries are washing and grooming products, of which soap is the typical example.

clue.text: Democrat leaders fiddle about with kings: they get more to watch

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the instrument goes round the party letters

parts.note: a fiddle is a violin
the leading letters of Democrat
K is king in chess notation, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Party bosses mess about with monarchs, giving the public more spectacle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle about' suggests messing around, but fiddle is the instrument and about is the wrapping instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Video links connect distant places by live camera feed, so they let people see more than they otherwise could.

clue.text: See 17
Play about church gains currency

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the play wraps round the church

parts.note: a play is a drama
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A play with a religious theme turns out to be timely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currency' looks like topicality but means money.
explanation.definitionFit: The drachma was the Greek unit of money until the euro replaced it.

clue.text: What a course could do to back her keeping a slave

indicators.note: to back is to move backwards, so the combined letters are read from the end
to keep something is to hold it inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: taken as written
a serf was a feudal bondsman

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about what a racecourse might do to support a woman who owns a slave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests racing, but it is a training course: a refresher course brings skills back up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: A refresher course exists to revive and update knowledge, which is to renew or restore it.

clue.text: Fiddle of old with notes by 11 West

definitions.note: 11 is Dame, and the answer is the first name of Dame ... West

parts.note: the rebec is a medieval bowed string instrument
two notes of the musical scale

explanation.surface: An old violin with some written notes by a woman named West.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is DAME; Dame Rebecca West was a writer and journalist. Any letter from A to G is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebecca West, created a Dame in 1959, was the pen name of the British novelist and critic Cicily Fairfield.

clue.text: ,14,6 Old guard's speech going out is about dear old new chum F. Gump

parts.note: a fort guards; the old way of writing the possessive was 'the fort his'

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the friend's letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: re means about or concerning
lief is an archaic word for dear or beloved
taken as written
Forrest Gump was played on screen by Tom Hanks, or T. Hanks

explanation.surface: The words of a sentry leaving duty are said to concern a dear old friend and a film character.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also points to Hamlet's opening scene, where the guard Francisco speaks this line when relieved. Old possessives were written 'X his' for X's.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet, the sentry Francisco says this line as he is relieved of his watch and goes off duty.

clue.text: Ulster, special clothing article for Kruschev

definitions.note: the definition is the surname; the answer is his first name

parts.note: Northern Ireland, often called Ulster
kit is outfit or gear for a particular purpose
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A list of items including a special outfit from Northern Ireland intended for the Soviet leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Nikita was the forename of Khrushchev, the Soviet premier from 1958 to 1964.

clue.text: Reported limit to fuel causes unrest

indicators.note: something reported is spoken, so the word is replaced by one that is said the same way

parts.note: a term is a fixed limit of time
oil is a fuel

explanation.surface: News of a cap on fuel supplies sparks public disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Turmoil is a state of great disturbance, confusion or agitation, close in sense to unrest.

clue.text: Without stocking much of Gray's work, get pushed around

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the pushing word encloses the shortened work

parts.note: to barge is to shove one's way

indicators.note: much of a thing is most but not all of it, so the last letter goes

parts.note: Thomas Gray's famous poem is his Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

explanation.surface: Unless you stock most of Gray's poems in your shop, you will be jostled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without stocking' reads like failing to keep goods in stock; it means not wearing stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare-legged means having the legs uncovered, wearing no stockings or tights.

clue.text: Journey before the fall

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an outing or excursion
second meaning: the stumble that comes just before you tumble

explanation.walkthrough: 'Before the fall' echoes 'pride comes before a fall' and the season of autumn, but it means the stumble that precedes a tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for an excursion and the stumble on a step that sends you to the ground.

clue.text: After shake-up, the unassertive become just the opposite

definitions.note: the opposite of the unassertive, an adjective

indicators.note: shaking jumbles things, so the two letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
shy people are unassertive

explanation.surface: After a reorganisation, timid staff turn into their own opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shake-up' reads as a reorganisation; split it into an anagram signal and its fodder. 'After' puts the timid word after that.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushy means forceful and self-assertive, the reverse of being timid or retiring.

clue.text: Writer drunk as a monkey?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pen name of the Edwardian short-story writer H. H. Munro
second meaning: a long-tailed South American primate

explanation.surface: A query whether some author is as drunk as a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' is a sly extra: the answer is also a variant spelling of sake, the Japanese rice wine, so it can be drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector Hugh Munro wrote under this pen name, and the same word names a bushy-tailed Amazonian primate.

clue.text: Porter (11 27) was born male, clad in blue

definitions.note: the answer completes 'Dame Shirley Porter, born ...', her maiden name

indicators.note: something clad in a garment is covered by it, so one word is wrapped by the other

parts.note: blue is the colour of the Conservatives, and CON abbreviates Conservative
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A biographical note: Dame Shirley Porter was born a boy and dressed in blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Dame Shirley Porter, Tesco heiress and Conservative leader of Westminster Council, was born into the Cohen family; blue is the Tory colour, apt for her.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirley Porter's maiden name was Cohen; she was the daughter of Tesco founder Sir Jack Cohen.

clue.text: Irregular French saint coming in to us

indicators.note: the saint is coming in, entering the other phrase and sitting inside it

parts.note: in French 'to us' is à nous, the French carrying over from the saint
Saint-Malo is the Breton port named after a French saint

explanation.surface: An unconventional French holy man arrives to join us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' serves both the saint and the phrase 'to us', which is turned into French. The saint goes in after the first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Anomalous means deviating from the norm or what is expected, a close synonym of irregular.

clue.text: Eliot is a fool? Putting it the other way helps

indicators.note: the words of the question are to be set out in the opposite order before joining

parts.note: an ass is a fool
taken as written
the poet T. S. Eliot is known by his initials

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the poet Eliot is an idiot, then tries saying it differently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eliot is a fool' becomes 'a fool is Eliot': swap the order of the words, not the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To assist is to aid or help, so 'assists' matches 'helps' as a third-person verb.

clue.text: Novel way of exchanging lire to chuck about

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for throwing goes round the rearranged money

parts.note: to shy is to throw

indicators.note: exchanging swaps things around, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the old Italian currency

explanation.surface: A new method of changing Italian money is to fling it about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new; it is the noun, a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirley is Charlotte Bronte's 1849 book, her second published work of fiction.
